title: What Is Money?
concept: Money is a commonly accepted medium of exchange that makes trading goods and services easier.
learningObjective: Understand why money exists and how it makes exchanging goods and services easier.
secondaryMisconceptions: Bartering always results in a fair and successful trade.
Money is useful only because coins and banknotes have physical value.
keyTakeaway: Money makes exchange easier because people agree to accept it.

screens.title: A Trade That Will Not Work
screens.content: You want Aisha’s bicycle, but she does not want your cricket bat. How can you make a trade you both accept?
screens.illustration: Two children face each other. One holds a cricket bat; the other stands beside a bicycle. A thought bubble shows a question mark between them.

screens.title: The Offer
screens.content: You offer Aisha your cricket bat for her bicycle. The bat is in good condition, so the swap seems possible.
screens.illustration: The learner holds out the cricket bat while pointing hopefully toward Aisha’s bicycle.

screens.title: No Match
screens.content: Aisha already has a bat. She would rather have money for art supplies. Your useful bat is not useful to her right now.
screens.illustration: Aisha gestures toward a bat she already owns and imagines paintbrushes and a sketchbook.

screens.title: What Would You Try?
screens.question: Which idea is most likely to help both people agree?

options.text: Swap the bat for the bicycle anyway
options.response: The bat may be valuable, but Aisha still does not want it.

options.text: Use money that both people accept
options.response: Good thinking. A shared way to pay could connect two different wants.

options.text: Say the bat and bicycle are equal
options.response: Calling them equal does not make Aisha want the bat or agree to the swap.

screens.title: Build the Trade Chain
screens.instruction: Arrange the four events from the problem to the result.

events.text: They cannot agree on what to exchange.

relationships.explanation: Wanting to trade is not enough when each person wants something different.
Money gives them something commonly accepted to exchange.
Each person can accept money and then use it in another trade.

alternativeContributingFactors: Both people still need to agree on the amount.
They need to trust that other people will also accept the money.
The item or service must still be available.
config.simplification: Money usually makes exchange easier, but it does not guarantee a fair price or a successful deal.
config.validationMethod: Check the full order after the learner submits. Accept only the defined sequence.
config.retryBehavior: Keep correctly placed events in position, gently highlight the first misplaced event, and allow unlimited retries.

accessibilityAlternative.method: Provide numbered selection controls and Move Up or Move Down buttons instead of requiring drag gestures.
accessibilityAlternative.screenReaderInstruction: Choose an event, assign its position from 1 to 4, then submit the sequence.

feedback.success: That chain works. Money connects people who want different things, so the exchange is easier.
feedback.incorrect: Almost. Start with the reason people need a trade, then find what solves the stuck exchange.
feedback.incomplete: Place all four events before checking the chain.

screens.title: Money Connects Different Wants
screens.content: You arranged a chain: people wanted to trade, the direct swap failed, they used money, and trading became easier. Money is a commonly accepted medium of exchange. People accept it when buying and selling, even when they do not want each other’s items. A £20 note is useful mainly because people trust others will accept it—not because its paper is worth £20. Money helps exchange value; it does not automatically create wealth or guarantee a fair price.
screens.simpleSummary: Money works because people agree to accept it for exchange.
screens.illustration: A £20 note forms a bridge between a cricket bat and a bicycle, with arrows showing two separate exchanges.

screens.title: At the School Fair
screens.content: One child sells a book for £3 and uses the £3 to buy a snack from another stall. The snack seller did not need the book; accepting money lets both exchanges happen.
screens.illustration: A child sells a book at one school-fair stall, then uses three £1 coins at a snack stall.

questions.text: Mia sells a puzzle for £4, then uses the £4 to buy pencils. What made both exchanges easier?

options.feedback: Correct. The same money could be accepted in two different exchanges.
The puzzle stayed a puzzle. Mia exchanged it for money that another seller accepted.
Mia paid £4 for the pencils, so they were not free.
Money helped Mia exchange value, but one trade did not automatically make her wealthy.

questions.correctExplanation: Money worked as a shared way to pay. The puzzle buyer and pencil seller both accepted £4, even though they wanted different items.
questions.misconceptionTested: Money is useful only because coins and banknotes have physical value.

questions.text: A pretend town prints twice as much money but makes no extra food, bicycles, or services. Is it automatically twice as wealthy?

options.feedback: More money by itself does not create extra useful goods or services.

options.text: No, extra money alone adds no goods or services
options.feedback: Correct. Real wealth depends on useful goods, services, skills, and resources—not just having more money.

options.text: Yes, because notes have physical value
options.feedback: The paper itself is not what makes a note worth its printed amount. Shared acceptance gives it its main use.

questions.correctExplanation: Money helps people exchange and measure value. Simply creating more money does not automatically create more useful goods, services, skills, or resources.

questions.text: Zara wants Noah’s comic. Noah does not want Zara’s stickers, but he will accept £3. What could Zara do?

options.text: Find a sticker buyer, receive £3, then buy the comic
options.feedback: Correct. Money can connect two separate exchanges when a direct swap does not work.
A trade needs agreement. Money can help, but it cannot replace consent.

options.text: Say the stickers and £3 are identical
options.feedback: They are different things. The useful point is that Noah agrees to accept the £3.
That is not a trade. Both people must agree before an exchange happens.

questions.correctExplanation: Zara can exchange the stickers with someone who wants them, then use commonly accepted money to buy the comic from Noah.
questions.misconceptionTested: Bartering always results in a fair and successful trade.

screens.headline: Exchange Explorer!
screens.message: You discovered how money helps people trade even when they want different things.
screens.progressMessage: Mission 1 complete in Become Money Smart.
screens.nextMissionTeaser: Next, discover the different jobs money can do.
screens.animation: A cricket bat and bicycle slide apart as a trail of coins forms a bridge between them, followed by a small star burst.

screens.title: Spot Money’s Job
screens.instruction: Find two things at home that came from different sellers. Ask yourself: would both sellers have wanted the same item in a barter swap?

reviewChecklist.notes: Every screen focuses on money as a commonly accepted medium of exchange.
The mission explains exchange, acceptance, and the difference between money and real wealth.
It uses a bicycle, cricket bat, art supplies, a school fair, and simple language.
No returns or guarantees are discussed.
No stocks or market predictions are included.
Incorrect choices receive calm, instructional feedback.
The mission states that money does not guarantee a fair price or successful trade.
The UK setting uses pounds and familiar child-friendly objects, including a cricket bat.
The cause-and-effect sequence shows how money resolves a difficult direct swap.
The quiz addresses acceptance, wealth creation, physical value, and failed barter.

reviewChecklist.item: Mission can be completed in under five minutes
reviewChecklist.notes: The mission is designed for approximately four minutes with one short ordering interaction and three quiz questions.

reviewChecklist.item: Language matches the target reading level
reviewChecklist.notes: Sentences are short, concrete, and suitable for ages 8–12.
